messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Anna Weber, a 35-year-old counselor, came to treatment months after a car accident in which another person was seriously injured. She had been driving home after a long day, replaying difficult conversations with clients, when she moved through an intersection and struck a cyclist she had not seen in time. What remained with her was not a single continuous memory but jagged fragments: the sudden shape in front of her headlights, the sound of impact, a bicycle wheel twisted at an impossible angle, someone shouting for an ambulance. She could not put the sequence together into a clear story, even privately. When the memory broke through, it brought a wave of grief so intense it felt almost physical, as if she were back at the roadside knowing that someone else’s life had been permanently altered.

From the beginning, Anna had come to believe that the injury happened because of the way she acted. She was certain she should have protected the cyclist and failed. That conviction was not abstract; it lived in the way she talked about herself, as someone who had done harm when she should have been the person who prevented it. Over time, those thoughts darkened into a broader sense that nothing in her life held meaning anymore. The more she judged herself as unforgivably responsible, the more on edge she became. Nights were the worst: she lay awake replaying what she did and did not do, flooded with guilt and horror, listening for every sound outside the house as if danger were still close.

Her work as a counselor made this especially hard to contain. She was used to meeting clients with direct attention, but after the accident she began avoiding eye contact in session, looking down at her notes or toward the clock because another person’s gaze made her feel exposed and accused. In the medical office building where she worked, the distant sound of an ambulance outside or seeing a patient arrive with a brace was enough to make her body tense before she had fully registered why. She became superalert in those moments, scanning hallways, flinching at sirens, feeling a sick rush of dread and shame. That state of watchfulness fed her conviction that she was dangerous or morally ruined, and each fresh surge of fear seemed to confirm that the accident had revealed something terrible about her.

The memory itself remained disorganized in part because Anna fought so hard against it. When images of the intersection surfaced, she tried immediately to push them away and not think about the trauma at all. She also began going out of her way to avoid hospitals, ambulances, and even routine physical examinations, because any medical cue could bring back the bicycle, the shouting, the sense of irreversible injury. In the short term that helped her get through the day, but it left the event sealed off in disconnected pieces. Because she would not linger with the memory, she never arrived at a fuller account of what happened; instead the fragments returned abruptly, each one carrying the same raw grief.

Her sense of threat and her efforts to manage it gradually tightened around each other. The more frightened, guilty, and keyed up she felt, the more she suppressed thoughts and steered away from medical reminders and from the eyes of other people. Those habits narrowed her world. She started taking longer routes to work to avoid passing the hospital entrance. At home, her husband noticed that she would turn away during conversations, especially if he asked about the accident or about how she was doing. Sleep grew more broken. In the small hours, hypervigilant and exhausted, the fragmented images were harder to keep out, and because they arrived without context they felt immediate and unbearable. Each recurrence left her more shaken the next day, more determined not to think, and less able to make sense of what had happened.

Over the months, that pattern deepened her despair. Being unable to form a coherent story made the accident feel unfinished and ever-present, which kept her body on guard; feeling constantly on guard only strengthened her belief that she had failed in the most basic duty to protect another person. By the time Anna sought help, she was still going to work but doing so mechanically, with a growing fear that she could sit compassionately with clients while feeling that her own life no longer meant anything. What finally brought her in was realizing she had begun avoiding a routine medical appointment and then crying in her car when she heard an ambulance pass. She said she was afraid that if she ever let herself remember the whole event, the guilt would destroy her, but she was also beginning to hope that if she could finally face it, the memory might stop ruling every part of her life.
